column1: Why can a single sensor reading not be the unit of prediction in wearable stress detection?
column2: Stress is a pattern over time. A heart rate of 92 at one instant could be a stressed nurse sitting still or a calm nurse climbing stairs.

column1: Why is accuracy a poor primary metric on the nurse stress dataset?
column2: About 80% of windows are labelled stress, so a model that always predicts "stressed" scores 0.80 while being worthless.

column1: Why is a random train/test split wrong when sliding windows overlap?
column2: Adjacent windows share up to half their raw rows, so a test window is nearly a duplicate of a training window. The reported score becomes fictitious.

column1: What is the rule of thumb for choosing a cross-validation split?
column2: Split along the axis you want to generalize across. If deployment means a new patient, hold out patients. If it means a new day, hold out days.

column1: Why does per-subject normalization matter more here than the usual "put features on a common scale" motivation?
column2: One person's resting heart rate can equal another's high-stress heart rate. Global scaling makes identical feature values carry opposite labels.

column1: Why did the global models fail in the nurse stress paper?
column2: Inter-individual physiological differences. Once data is pooled across nurses, the same feature values correspond to different labels depending on whose wrist they came from.

column1: What is wrong with tuning a decision threshold on the test set?
column2: It is implicit validation leakage. The test set has influenced a modelling decision, so it is no longer held out and the reported score is optimistic.

column1: What three-way split fixes decision-threshold leakage?
column2: Train days to fit the model, a calibration split to choose the threshold, and a test split that is touched exactly once to report the score.

column1: Why must rates of change be supplied to a tree model as explicit columns?
column2: Trees split on thresholds of the features you give them. They cannot compute a derivative, so if you want the model to reason about change, change must be a feature.

column1: Why include accelerometer data in a physiological stress model?
column2: Confounder control. Physical exertion raises heart rate and sweating exactly like stress does, so the model needs a channel that separates the two.

column1: What are the two things you can do with a window, and which models does each enable?
column2: Summarize it into a fixed-length vector, which enables trees, XGBoost and MLPs. Or keep the full sequence, which enables CNNs and LSTMs.

column1: What is lost when a window is summarized into 24 summary statistics?
column2: The shape of the signal. A window that rises smoothly and one that spikes then recovers can have identical means, standard deviations and endpoints.

column1: What does GlobalAveragePooling1D do, and what is the point of it?
column2: It averages each filter's response across all timesteps. This deliberately discards where a pattern occurred and keeps only whether it occurred.

column1: What different inductive biases do a 1D CNN and an LSTM encode?
column2: The CNN asks whether a characteristic local shape appears anywhere in the window. The LSTM asks what the state of the signal is after reading the whole sequence in order.

column1: Why does binarizing three stress levels into two improve the metric while narrowing usefulness?
column2: Level 1 is too rare for a model to learn, so collapsing it helps measured performance. The model can then no longer separate mild strain from acute crisis, which is the distinction a deployed system would most want.

column1: Name four techniques for handling class imbalance during training.
column2: Class weights in the loss function, weighted sampling so batches are balanced, undersampling the majority class, and focal loss.

column1: Why is SMOTE questionable on time-series windows?
column2: It generates synthetic examples by interpolating between real neighbors, and interpolating between two physiological states can produce a window that is not physiologically possible.

column1: What is the difference between prediction and causal inference?
column2: Prediction asks what will happen given what I observe. Causal inference asks what would happen if I intervened. A feature can improve prediction while pointing the wrong way causally.

column1: What makes time-to-event analysis distinct from classification?
column2: The question is when an event happens rather than whether it happens, and censoring means some subjects' events are never observed at all.

column1: When is anomaly detection preferable to classification for wearable data?
column2: When labels are scarce or unreliable. You model each person's normal and flag departures from it, which requires no self-reported labels.

column1: What is multilabel classification, and where is it commonly misfiled?
column2: Predicting any number of answers at once. ICD code assignment is multilabel because a patient can carry many diagnoses, yet it is often built as multiclass.

column1: Why is PR-AUC preferred over ROC-AUC under heavy class imbalance?
column2: ROC-AUC can look flatteringly high when the negative class is rare, because the false positive rate has a large denominator that hides errors.

column1: What does "idealized" mean in the idealized per-nurse random forest?
column2: Folds that fail quality checks are discarded, so the 0.859 is an upper bound on achievable performance under favorable data conditions, not an estimate of deployed performance.

column1: How is transfer learning applied in the 1D CNN pipeline?
column2: Train the network on other subjects, freeze the convolutional layers, then re-fit only the dense head on a slice of the held-out subject's own data.

column1: Why must the fine-tuning slice be chronological rather than random?
column2: A random slice would let the model see the future of the very recording it is about to be evaluated on.

column1: What is the fourth main learning paradigm alongside supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning?
column2: Self-supervised learning, where labels are invented from the data itself and the learned representation is then reused for a real task with few labels.
